conservation.notes: As a sagebrush obligate the species depends on sagebrush for nesting and is therefore vulnerable to habitat loss, including wildfire fragmentation and conversion of shrubsteppe to urban or agricultural land.

human_tolerance.notes: Shrubsteppe 'converted into urban development or agricultural land hav[e] historically caused local extirpation of the species in some of its range', and annual grass cover such as cheatgrass is negatively associated with the species nesting. It needs big sagebrush, not a built garden.

phases.name: absent
phases.note: 'migrates south to southern United States and northern Mexico for winter'.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: The cup nest is built in or under big sagebrush; both sexes incubate the clutch of four to five eggs.

phases.name: young
phases.note: The species defends its territory through song, undulating flight displays and chase flight by pursuing intruders through the nesting season.

vocalizations.description: The song the male uses to defend its breeding territory, delivered with undulating flight displays and followed by chase flight against intruders; no open source gives a rendering of it.
A short harsh note used as contact and alarm; the call_id and this rendering are authored, because the article describes song and displays but does not itemise the calls.

taxonomy.note: GBIF's match returns Oreoscoptes montanus (Townsend, 1837) as ACCEPTED; the article's taxonomy section records the 1837 description by John Kirk Townsend and that the genus is monotypic. Family Mimidae is the article's.

external.note: gbif_usage_key is the ACCEPTED key from the GBIF species match for Oreoscoptes montanus; inat_taxon_id is the iNaturalist taxon returned by the API match. Optional keys (ITIS TSN, Wikidata Q-number, eBird code) were not looked up, so they are omitted rather than guessed.

conservation.note: The IUCN status is recorded as LC. The threats material is quoted from the article's own Threats section, which describes sagebrush dependence and habitat loss but does not itself state a Red List category, so the category should be confirmed against IUCN directly if a reviewer needs the citation.

range.note: 'breeding from the Great Basin to southern British Columbia, and migrates south to southern United States and northern Mexico for winter'; in the United States 'from central Washington southward through eastern Oregon and the northeastern part of California', east across Nevada, Utah and western Colorado. US, CA and MX are given as native, covering the annual range. koppen is omitted: the article gives no climate classification, only the shrubsteppe habitat.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Honest gap: the article gives length and mass but no wingspan, and no wingspan figure was found on Wikidata or GBIF for this item. 0.29 m is an authored estimate from the bird's length (0.215 m) and the wing-aspect ratio of a small thrush, so a reviewer should replace it with a measured wingspan if one becomes available.

traits.lifespan_y.note: No sourced typical or mean lifespan figure was found for this species in the English Wikipedia article, on Wikidata or in GBIF. Estimated by analogy to similarly sized open-country passerines already in this repository with a sourced figure (Eurasian blackbird ~3 y from ring-recovery statistics), which show the high first-year mortality typical of small songbirds; 3.0 y is used as a conservative, unsourced judgement pending a better source.

traits.diet.note: 'primarily forage on the ground feeding, feeding mainly on terrestrial insects' - ants, ground beetles, true bugs, grasshoppers and crickets - with the added statement that the species 'can also eat berries and seeds'. invertebrate 0.8 follows 'mainly'; fruit and seed shares are an authored judgement from that last sentence, with fruit above seed because berries are named first.

traits.social.note: A cup nest with a clutch of four to five eggs in which 'both sexes contribute in the incubation process', and territory defence by the pair through song, display and chase flight, describe a monogamous breeder. The article does not describe winter flocking, so Flock is not recorded.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Judgement: diurnal. Foraging, nest building and the described territorial song and flight displays are day-time activity, and the article notes the bird places its nest to take advantage of cooler air and to avoid the day's most intense sun, which implies daytime heat avoidance rather than nocturnality.

traits.defense.note: 'the sage thrasher defend their territory through song, undulating flight displays, and chase flight by pursuing intruders' - active displacement of a threat rather than freezing or hiding, but the response is flight-based, so Flee is recorded.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The nest is cup-shaped, about 10 cm in height and 18-20 cm in diameter'. Cup is the matching enum value.

traits.perching.note: The bird defends its territory by song from the shrub it nests in and performs undulating flight displays from and back to vegetation; a shrubsteppe songbird's ordinary posture is perched on a bush.

traits.note: Grouped entries. body_plan Vertebrate, limb_count 2, thermoregulation Endotherm, skin Feathers, respiration Lungs and metamorphosis None are the standard bird values the article's description of a passerine implies. flight Powered follows the bird's undulating and chase flight displays. size_class Tiny is derived from mass_kg (under 0.05 kg). locomotion_modes Walk, Hop and Fly: the bird forages on the ground, perches in shrubs and makes sustained display flights.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement set mid-range: the species is described as an aggressive territory defender that pursues intruders, yet it is tied to dense sagebrush cover and suffers local extirpation where habitat is converted, and its nests are placed to conceal them from aerial predators. flight_distance_m 30 m reflects a bird that drops into cover rather than fleeing far.

habitat.use.note: Authored from the habitat and diet sections: 'primarily forage on the ground' in shrubsteppe 'dominated by big sagebrush', with the bird nesting in or under the shrub and displaying from it. Ground and shrub therefore split the use roughly evenly, with a small aerial share for the display flights.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'The sage thrasher typically nest in big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) and three-tip sagebrush (A. tripartita)', in the densest parts of the vegetation. shrub_thicket is the matching ResourceTag, and the dependence is total: the species is described as a sagebrush obligate.

habitat.resources.note: invertebrate 0.8 follows 'mainly on terrestrial insects'; fruit 0.15 and seed 0.05 follow 'can also eat berries and seeds'. shrub_thicket 1.0 reflects the total nesting dependence on sagebrush. perch 0.8 reflects song and display perches in the nesting shrub.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Avoider and uses_gardens false follow the threats section: shrubsteppe 'converted into urban development or agricultural land hav[e] historically caused local extirpation', and cheatgrass cover is 'negatively associated with occurrence of sage thrasher for nesting'. light_max 0.3 and flight_distance_m 30 m are authored judgements for a bird that needs undisturbed open shrubsteppe.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'breeding from the Great Basin to southern British Columbia, and migrates south to southern United States and northern Mexico for winter'. Migration is the enum value for a species that breeds in one region and winters in another.

seasonal.phases.note: Honest gap, filled with judgement: the article states that the species migrates south for the winter and describes the nest and clutch, but gives no incubation length, no nestling period and no calendar dates for any phase. The absent window is the complement of a western-breeding / southern-wintering bird, and the nesting and young windows are an authored judgement placed around a normal passerine breeding season in eastern Oregon. A reviewer should replace these with the dates in a nest-record source if one is available.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The article gives the clutch size ('four to five eggs', each 'averaging 25 mm in length and 4.3g in mass') and that both sexes incubate, but no incubation or nestling duration. Egg and Juvenile durations are therefore authored judgements for a small passerine, not quoted figures. scale is authored.

vocalizations.thrasher_song.note: 'During the breeding season, the sage thrasher defend their territory through song, undulating flight displays, and chase flight by pursuing intruders.' The song's existence, season and function are quoted; the description sentence says explicitly that no open source gives a rendering of the song, so time windows and the cooldown are authored.

vocalizations.chack.note: Honest gap, filled with a judgement: the article describes song, undulating flight displays and chase flight, but does not itemise a contact or alarm call, so the call_id and its Contact mapping are authored rather than quoted.

look.note: Colours from the description section: 'Adults display brownish-gray upperparts and white underparts marked with dark streaks', with 'eyes ... distinctive ranging from lemon-yellow to amber'. The palette maps brownish-grey to body, white to belly, the dark streaks to markings and the lemon-yellow eye to eye, with accent holding the lemon-yellow of the eye ring. The streaked underparts are an extra part on the breast. The 'shorter and less curved bill, shorter tail and smaller size' that distinguish it from other thrashers set beak_ratio and tail_ratio below the values used for a large thrasher. Proportions are otherwise authored.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: ground foraging on terrestrial insects, a moderate flee distance for a bird that drops into sagebrush cover, a nest window matching an April-July sagebrush nesting season, and call ids matching the vocalizations above. The program is a reasonable fit: this is a small perching passerine that forages on the ground by hopping and perches in shrubs to sing.
